title: Diaries of a Primitive Man

body:
Weekly Newsletter
                John Yau on Roy Lichtenstein, Megan O’Grady on John Berger, and Paddy Johnson answers the question: Do I need an agent?
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Jackson Pollock, "Number 13A: Arabesque" (1948) (photo Hakim BIshara/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            It’s a sunny October afternoon in Manhattan and the steps of the Metropolitan Museum of Art are bustling with visitors. Tourists pose for selfies against the museum’s facade; street vendors sell chopped-up hotdogs in a nest of French fries; and the sound of saxophone music drowns into the symphony of splashing water fountains and honking cars on Fifth Avenue. So many types of people; the only ones missing are the Lenape whose land was stolen so we could enjoy this fine Indigenous Peoples’ Day on the steps of The Met. Inside the museum, a blockbuster exhibition about Abstract Expressionist painters Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock is jam-packed. The show is as much about their mutual influence as it is about their marriage, their most difficult collaboration. I hear a woman from behind accusing me of “White privilege” because I apparently cut her in line. I turn around and say, “What White privilege? Look at me.” She takes a quick look and corrects herself, “Okay, so male privilege.”I turn on Democracy Now and listen to a 30-minute conversation about settler colonialism. I notice a Jeep Wrangler ahead of me with a sticker proudly announcing, “primitive man.” I shudder at first but quickly come to admire the driver’s honesty. War Secretary Pete Hegseth threatens to livestream an execution by firing squad. At the Brooklyn Museum, I pause by a display of Indigenous Kachina dolls that were given to Hopi girls and women living in what is now Arizona. Who made them and how they got here we don’t exactly know, but now they belong to the museum’s Center for Feminist Art. At the end of the day, my shoulders are tense and my brain cooked, and my only wish is to lie down idea-free, opinionless, primitive.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief 

	
		
			Roy Lichtenstein Has Lost His Luster
		
	
	
	Roy Lichtenstein’s paintings stick in your mind. They are memorable and congenial. When I went to Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, the first major survey of his work in more than 30 years, at the Whitney Museum, I expected to be surprised by something new the curators dug up in their research into the sources of many of the more than 130 paintings, sculptures, drawings, and prints on view. I was not initially disappointed. | John Yau

		John Berger in His Own Bruised Time
		
	
	
	The late novelist and art critic asked Tom Overton to wait to write his biography until after his death. The result is deeply informative, deferential, and perceptive, sometimes lyrically so. | Megan O’Grady

		Finding Vermeer in Unexpected Places
		
	
	
		Artists, filmmakers, poets, and the art market itself still bear traces of the Dutch painter’s influence, writes historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell in “Vermeer’s Afterlives.” | Lauren Moya Ford

title: Eight Galleries in India You Should Know
body:
Home
	

				
							
					
	
	ARTnews
	

				
							
					
	
	Market
	

				
						

		
									
	October 17, 2026 3:00am	
					
							
		
			
				

			
			
			
	
			
					Installation view of "Amol K Patil: A Forest of Remembrance," 2025, at Project 88.
									Photo Anil Rane/Courtesy the artist and Project 88
	


				

	The Indian contemporary art market has been on an upswing in recent years. The growth has been catalyzed by the country’s economic boom and explosion in private wealth. This has been amplified by a surge in prices for the work of India’s modern masters, now nearly inaccessible for emerging collectors. Galleries have been in rapid expansion mode, participating in more art fairs internationally, and opening new spaces.

	Below is a primer looking at eight of India’s top galleries, whose programs are influential and at times cutting-edge. Listed alphabetically, the featured galleries regularly participate in leading international art fairs, have placed the work of their artists in major institutions, or represent artists who frequently appear on the biennial circuit.


			
			
	Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai
			
										
					Image Credit: Anil Rane/Courtesy Chemould Prescott Road				
					
				

	Founded in 1963, Chemould Prescott Roadisa third-generation gallery now helmed by Shireen Gandhy. Cultivated over the past three decades, its roster includes some of India’s most recognized contemporary artists, including Mithu Sen, Jitish Kallat, Shilpa Gupta, and NS Harsha, as well as younger artists like Mohit Shelare, Naresh Kumar, and Karan Shrestha, who joined the gallery in February. A regular exhibitor at Art Basel since 2010, Gandhy sat on the selection committee for the inaugural edition of Art Basel Qatar, held this past February. Locally, the dealer has also been a driving force of Mumbai Gallery Weekend since its inception in 2012. A fourth generation is also involved in the gallery: Gandhy’s daughter, Atyaan Jungalwala, runs the offshoot space Chemould CoLab, which represents artists like Jayeeta Chatterjee and Gurjeet Singh.

	Address: 3rd floor, Queens Mansion, Ghanshyam Talwatkar Marg, Azad Maidan, Fort, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400001, India

		
			
			
	Experimenter, Kolkata and Mumbai
			
										
					Image Credit: Vivienne Sarky/Courtesy Experimenter				
					
				

	Founded by Prateek and Priyanka Raja in 2009, Experimenter quickly built a reputation for supporting alternative artistic practices often focused on photography and film, mixed media, and found objects. While Kolkata is often disconnected from art market hubs like Mumbai and Delhi, the gallery has approached that situation through an aggressive presence at leading art fairs, like Art Basel in Basel and Hong Kong, Frieze London New York, and FIAC in Paris. Prateek currently sits on the selection committee for Art Basel in Basel, Switzerland, while Priyanka does the same at Art Dubai. In 2018, it opened a second space in Kolkata and then in 2022 expanded to Mumbai. In 2025, they added a third outpost in Kolkata, inside the historical, colonial-era Alipore Jail, which has been renovated and repurposed as a cultural space. They have also organised a Curator’s Hub since 2010 which has drawn top curators like Doryun Chong, Hans Ulrich Obrist, Adam Szymczyk, and Naomi Beckwith. The roster includes a diverse range of South Asian and diaspora voices like Naeem Mohamien, Sanchayan Ghosh, Sakshi Gupta, Prabhakar, Pushpakanthan Pakkiyarajah, and Sohrab Hura, who is included in the 2026 Venice Biennale.

	Address: 2/1, Hindustan Road, Dover Terrace, Ballygunge, Kolkata, West Bengal 700019, India

		
			
			
	Jhaveri Contemporary, Mumbai
			
										
					Image Credit: Mohammed Chiba/Courtesy Jhaveri Contemporary				
					
				

	Amrita Jhaveri helped set up Christie’s office in India in the mid-1990s and led it for a few years before moving to London, where she worked as an adviser managing private and corporate art collections. In 2010, she cofounded Jhaveri Contemporary with her sister Priya in Mumbai. The gallery moving to its current space, facing the Gateway of India in 2018. Its roster includes a mix of well-known contemporary artists from the South Asian diaspora, including Rana Begum, Lubna Chowdhary, Permindar Kaur, Shezad Dawood, and Mathew Krishanu, as well as the estates of post-modern artists like Mrinalini Mukherjee, Raghubir Singh, Balraj Khanna, Anwar Jalal Shemza, and Zahoor Ul Akhlaq.

	Address: 3rd Floor, Devidas Mansion, 4 B K Boman Behram Marg, Apollo Bandar, Colaba, Mumbai 400001, India 

		
			
			
	Nature Morte, New Delhi, Delhi, and Mumbai
			
										
					Image Credit: Akik Rahaman/Courtesy the artists and Nature Morte				
					
				

	Nature Morte has umbilical ties to New York. Cofounded by American artist and curator Peter Nagy in East Village in the early 80s, it was reincarnated in 1997 in New Delhi after Nagy had moved there. In 2013, artist Aparajit Jain became a partner and director in the gallery, helping Nagy, who died in October 2026, take Nature Morte to new heights. In 2021, it moved to two new spaces in Delhi and then in 2024 it expanded to Mumbai. Its roster includes internationally recognised artists like Bharti Kher, Subodh Gupta, Imran Qureshi, Sagarika Sundaram, and Asim Waqif, who represented India at the 2026 Venice Biennale.

	Address: A-9, Block A, Gulmohar Park, New Delhi, 110049, India

		
			
			
	Project 88, Mumbai
			
										
					Image Credit: Anil Rane/Courtesy the artist and Project 88				
					
				

	Artists on gallerist Sree Banerjee Goswami’s roster have routinely found critical recognition in recent years. Rohini Devasher became the first Indian artist to be named Artist of the Year by Deutsche Bank in 2024, the same year Khandakar Ohida won the V&A’s Jameel Prize. Neha Choksi, who like Devasher has been with Project 88 since its inception in 2006, saw the entirety of her last solo at gallery acquired by the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art (KNMA). And Goswami began representing Amol Patil, just before he showed at Documenta 15 in 2022. Other key artists include Delhi-based RAQS Media Collective who also curated the 2016 Shanghai Biennale, and Baroda-based painter Mahesh Baliga.

	Address: Ground Floor, BMP Building, N.A. Sawant Marg (Narayan A Sawant Road), Colaba, Mumbai – 400 005, Maharashtra, India

		
			
			
	Talwar Gallery, New York and New Delhi
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Ranjani Shettar/Courtesy Talwar Gallery, New York and New Delhi/The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York				
					
				

	Founded by Deepak Talwar in New York in 2001 and with a second location in New Delhi since 2007, Talwar Gallery has championed art from the Indian subcontinent with several milestones to its credit, from staging Nasreen Mohamedi’s first solo in the US in 2003 to debuting, in 2017, Arpita Singh’s early turn to abstraction in 2017. What sets the gallery apart is tighter artist roster of 13 and a focus on doing fewer shows with longer runs, typically six months, allowing them to focus on cultivating relationships with institutions and collectors as opposed to participating in numerous art fairs each year. One such example is artist Ranjani Shettar whom Talwar started representing two decades ago when she was in her 20s and whose works he has placed in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, and the San Francisco Museum of Art.

	Address: C-84 Neeti Bagh, New Delhi – 110049 India

		
			
			
	TARQ, Mumbai
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy TARQ				
					
				

	In 2014 when she was only 25, Hena Kapadia founded TARQ in the Dhanraj Mahal, a heritage building that is home to the Mumbai outposts of Christie’s and Nature Morte. To match the gallery’s growth, she moved to a larger 3000–square-foot space in the city’s Fort neighborhood in 2022. The gallery’s participation in Art Basel Hong Kong since 2018 has led to increased exposure of its artists in East Asia, with M+ acquiring works by Sameer Kulavoor and Parag Tandel. Its roster also includes photographers Ronny Sen and Phillipe Calia, textile artists Boshudhara Mukherjee and Areez Katki, printmaker Soghra Khorasani, painter Rithika Merchant, and draughtsman Vishva Shroff.

	Address: Ground Floor, KK (Navsari) Chambers, 39/39B AK Nayak Marg, Fort, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400001, India 

		
			
			
	Vadehra Art Gallery, New Delhi
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Vadehra Art Gallery				
					
				

	Founded in 1987, Vadehra Art Galleryestablished itself by championing modern masters, like M.F. Husain, S.H Raza, Yeb Mehta and Ram Kumar. Today, its roster also includes younger South Asian artists like Biraaj Dodiya, Zaam Arif and Ashfika Rehman. In 2011, it added a second space in New Delhi’s Defence Colony neighborhood. The gallery has regularly participated in Art Basel, Art Basel Hong Kong, and Frieze London, where it often stages pop-up shows at Frieze’s 9 Cork Street in Mayfair. Gallery artists like Gauri Gill and Sunil Gupta have had their work acquired by institutions like Tate and the Met, respectively. 

	Address: D-40, Block D, Defence Colony, New Delhi, Delhi 110024, India

		Good morning!	


The Norton Simon Museum countersued the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, following the latter’s suit claiming it owned a Nazi-looted Lucas Cranach diptych in the museum collection.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art has selected artist Danh Võ for its 2027 Genesis Façade Commission.
The Biennale Jogja Foundation in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, has announced it is closing its operations after 16 years, due to political and economic turmoil.


	
		The Headlines	

	CRANACH CONFUSION. The Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, California, countersued the Jewish Federation Los Angeles on Wednesday, following the latter’s suit claiming it owned a Nazi-looted Lucas Cranach diptych, Adam and Eve, made around 1530, in the museum’s collection, reports Courthouse News Service. The museum argues a previous federal lawsuit in its favor should override the Jewish Federation’s new attempt to assert ownership using a new California law allowing residents to revisit failed legal attempts to recuperate Nazi-looted art. The museum’s complaint states that “the finality of the prior von Saherjudgment is beyond dispute … this court found on the merits that the museum was the sole owner of the Cranachs.”

	
		Related Articles
	


	FACING UP. The Metropolitan Museum of Art has selected artist Danh Võ for its 2027 Genesis Façade Commission, reports ArtAsiaPacific. This will be the fourth presentation installed on the museum’s 5th Avenue Beaux-Arts façade, and the Vietnamese-born artist plans to exhibit four sculptures. “A façade is the place where the museum meets the street, and it is also an expression of its values over time,” Võ said in a statement. In addition, the Norwegian Congolese artist Sandra Mujinga was chosen to make a site-specific installation for the Met’s 2027 Great Hall Commission.
	
	
		The Digest	

	The Biennale Jogja Foundation in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, has announced it is closing its operations after 16 years of overseeing the Biennale Jogja, due to “a political regime” amid “chaotic economic and political policies, increasing censorship, and violence against activists and protesters.” [ArtAsiaPacific]

	Three years after it was removed, plans are in the works to return a restored 1914 Confederate memorial to Arlington National Cemetery, which includes the figure of a Black woman holding the child of a white officer and a slave following his owner to war. [NBC]
	

	The opening of the Centre Pompidou Paraná in southern Brazil has been delayed again amid a local government shift and is now expected to open in 2029. [The Art Newspaper]

	Australia has returned a 14,000-year-old carved stone slab to Jordan that was found in Wadi Al Hammah and taken to the National Gallery of Australia in 1985. [Menafn]

	Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza, the Spanish Baroness whose family’s private collection is exhibited in the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum in Madrid, is bringing to auction a 1944 painting of a sailboat at sea by Edward Hopper on November 18 at Sotheby’s in New York, with a high estimate of $30 million. [El Pais]

	Rubaiya Qatar, the new quadrennial on vie November 21 to April 30 in Doha, has revealed the full list of participating artists, who number over 120. [ArtReview]
	
		The Kicker	

	DEALING WITH DISASTER. William Kentridge talks to Ocula as his latest film premieres at London’s Goodman Gallery. Titled A Nicely Built City (Never Resists Destruction), the stop-animation film is accompanied by an exhibition of artworks. It looks at Johannesburg’s industrial transformation, and how wilderness returns to the city as its center collapses. Asked about using humor in his films, alongside the political weight of their subjects, Kentridge responded: “I don’t think there’s a contradiction between the serious and the light, and how the one illuminates the other. I think the category of the absurd is also important. Tragedy isn’t a good way of dealing with social disaster. Comedy may be closer, but the category of the absurd, which can move between the two, is central.” Read on to learn Kentridge’s thoughts on Anselm Kiefer’s “fantastic woodcuts,” the “poetic and politically powerful” art of Alfredo Jaar, his own studio process, and more.

The Best Booths at 1-54 London, From 3D-Printed Chairs to Futuristic Visions of Lagos’s Waterfront
		
									
	October 17, 2026 11:27am	
					
							
		
			
				

			
			
			
	
			
					A performance staged by the 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair at Somerset House, London. 
									Photo India Jane/Courtesy 1-54
	


				

	The 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair has returned to London for its 14th edition, which has introduced a new section this year focused on African modernism, curated by art historian Nancy Dantas. Titled “West Wind” and inspired by Miriam Makeba’s 1966 anthem for unity, this presentation addresses the gap left by Sotheby’s when it closed its dedicated African modernism department in 2025. The showcase features mid-20th-century masters, like Ibrahim El-Salahi, Bertina Lopes, and Seyni Awa Camara, celebrating a vibrant period of political and aesthetic liberation across the continent and its diaspora. With this, the fair looks to the future while also honoring the past, illuminating the continent’s rich cultural and artistic landscape.

	Below, a look at the 10 best booths at 1-54 London, which runs through Sunday at Somerset House.


			
			
	Ekene Emeka Maduka at Fabienne Levy
			
										
					Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews				
					
				
	Fabienne Levy presents seven paintings by Nigerian-born artist Ekene Emeka Maduka, who constructs a nostalgic “memory palace” rooted in her formative years at a Nigerian boarding school, as seen in the oil-on-canvas diptych Presence, Half-remembered (2026), showing three schoolgirls. Developed during a residency in Switzerland, these works serve as a microcosm of society, exploring themes of identity and displacement, and mark her artistic growth across Nigeria, Canada, and Switzerland. Rather than offering a direct autobiography, Maduka’s canvases immerse viewers in her subjects’ memories. The presentation contrasts the human figure with the architecture of a postcolonial modernist compound, positioning the school itself as a central protagonist. By juxtaposing Western literary influences such as William Golding’s Lord of the Flies with Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart, Maduka examines the alienating frameworks of neo-colonized education and discipline. The resulting dreamscapes carry a haunting quality that lingers, capturing how context-rich environments endure in the human psyche.
		
			
			
	Holly Rollins at Gillian Jason Gallery
			
										
					Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews				
					
				
	London-based artist, designer, and interior architect Holly Rollins explores the domestic space as an archive of cultural memory and diasporic knowledge. Her exhibition comprises four sets of works, including lamps, clay photo frames, and two chairs that blur the line between functional sculpture and fine art. At the center of the display is the pink-colored Kaymito Chair (2026), made from 3D-printed recycled plastic. Working under her studio ROLSTUDIO, Rollins reinterprets familiar household forms to stimulate care, intimacy, and intergenerational memory, drawing from Caribbean matrifocal family structures. A key aspect of her philosophy is material experimentation. She combines diverse media, such as clay and memory foam, with modular systems, as seen in her custom lighting pieces positioned on a glass table and pouffe stool. Rollins’s academic research into neuro-architecture and how spatial environments influence identity informs her creation of interactive objects. Ultimately, her layout turns the booth into a landscape where everyday design elements become tangible vessels of inheritance and belonging.
		
			
			
	Damilola Opedun at Yenwa Gallery
			
										
					Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews				
					
				
	At Yenwa Gallery’s booth, two paintings, The Sacred Between and The Center Between The Noise (both 2026), tell the story of a largely forgotten community. Damilola Opedunhighlights Makoko, a vulnerable waterfront community in Lagos, creating a visual dialogue with Venice’s historic canals. The paintings also document the devastating 2025 government demolitions and land reclamation projects that have displaced Makoko residents. Opedun’s multilayered oil paintings ask whether Makoko can have a future, imaging one where it becomes celebrated worldwide for its art scene and attractions, like Venice. Although the artist has never visited Venice, his works blend lived experiences with imaginative possibilities. Using a palette of blues and browns, these compositions feature a unique, cloudy bird’s-eye perspective that makes viewers feel as though they are surveying the landscape from above or sharing the artist’s vision of what lies on the other side. By intertwining Makoko’s floating structures with iconic Venetian landmarks like Santa Maria della Salute, Opedun uses light and architectural elements to blur geographic boundaries and reflect on how history, wealth, and culture shape how communities are valued.
		
			
			
	Buqaqawuli Nobakada at Affinity Gallery
			
										
					Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews				
					
				
	Cape Town–based artist Buqaqawuli Nobakada uses her mixed-media practice to look into “mass manifesting” abundance and leisure for Black women. Emcimbini (2026), for example, is a lace-on-canvas painting depicting a vibrant poolside scene with several women lounging on beach chairs and swimming. Having grown up witnessing the socio-economic restrictions and struggles faced by previous generations of women, Nobakada uses her art to project them into aspirational realities. Her canvases become a generational meeting place, allowing women to comfortably inhabit spaces of pleasure and freedom without needing permission. Rather than viewing manifestation as an individual pursuit, the artist frames it as a collective expansion of what is possible. By incorporating delicate lace, Nobakada adds a layer to these ordinary yet historically restricted moments of belonging, extending possibilities into the past and ensuring the women who shaped her experiences are included in these newly imagined futures of joy.
		
			
			
	Medhat Shafik at Errm Art Gallery
			
										
					Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews				
					
				
	Unveiling a new collection of texturally rich paintings, Egyptian artist Medhat Shafik applies art as a metaphor for the fractures in contemporary society. Working like an archaeologist, he merges pieces together in what he calls “fragments” to help society reconnect with a sense of collective identity amid global conflict. The booth’s centerpiece, a layered collage painting titled Red (2025), introduces the otherworldly into this discussion, as seen via an asteroid hurtling toward Earth in this red-dominated composition. His practice is rooted in mystery and draws inspiration from ancient Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Nile heritages. He builds his canvases from a variety of materials, including natural sand, teabags, and fabrics treated with Indian dyeing techniques. This focus on materiality gives the artwork an organic quality, inviting viewers to look beyond the surface and discover the hidden meanings behind the abstract shapes, revealing a shared human narrative.
		
			
			
	Yvanovitch Mbaya at Ablakassa
			
										
					Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews				
					
				
	Exploring themes of belonging, memory and cultural identity, Congolese artist Yvanovitch Mbaya’s massive textile showpiece, Untitled (2023), takes center stage in the room. Crafted from recycled denim, a fabric also used to cover trucks transporting commercial goods, Mbaya repurposes this rugged material as an homage to his people. On its surface, anonymous, genderless figures from the Bantu tribe appear. Using coffee and oil paint, he infuses the heavy denim with materials that create varied textures and an earthy presence. Also on view are two works on paper, demonstrating the artist’s multidisciplinary transition between canvas and paper. He also takes inspiration from his academic background in art psychology and his physical journeys across Africa. Mbaya’s installation balances individual memory, capturing how people and their material histories continuously shape one another.
		
			
			
	Mellaney Roberts at Berman Contemporary Gallery
			
										
					Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews				
					
				
	Mellaney Roberts, a ceramic artist and academic from South Africa, transforms clay, glass, and metal into vessels of remembrance. Originally from Willowmore in the Eastern Cape, Roberts has created three sculptures for the fair, exploring themes of identity, material memory, and land-based narratives. Her latest body of work emerges from a place of mourning following the devastating floods in May 2026, which washed away ancestral lands belonging to marginalized Coloured and Khoi communities in South Africa. To honor this history and repair fractured legacies, Roberts focuses on materiality, sourcing clay, resin, and tree bark collected from her home region. Her standing sculpture, Die Draers (The Bearers), 2026, has a touch of the steampunk aesthetic, integrating copper into the cut and pierced ceramic surfaces. The works function as metaphors for shifting cultural borders and classifications. Roberts’s hybrid forms conjure intergenerational memories, subverting discourses of otherness and challenging the painful feeling of non-belonging.
		
			
			
	Alpha Odhiambo at 16/16
			
										
					Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews				
					
				
	Self-taught, Nairobi-based artist Alpha Odhiambo presents a technical showcase of a unique painting method he’s spent years perfecting. He works exclusively on industrial vinyl mesh, as seen in his multilayered piece Bodybuilder (2026). Odhiambo meticulously mixes acrylics and solvent paints to achieve a precise viscosity that prevents pigment from seeping through the porous screen. The resulting work balances opacity and translucency, resembling stained-glass windows or shifting holograms. The piece also changes under different lighting conditions, adding to its dynamic nature. Odhiambo is inspired by the imagery from daily life to analyze global political structures and their impact on human livelihoods, with his layered mesh works serving as a mirror to power. He invites viewers to interpret his work and shows how technical precision can become a catalyst for critical societal engagement.
		
			
			
	Souad Abdelrasoul at Gallery Misr
			
										
					Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews				
					
				
	Artist and art historian Souad Abdelrasoul, who lives and works in Cairo, employs surreal, metamorphosed figures to explore the tension between progressive women and oppressive social and cultural systems. Her large-scale centerpiece painting, A Memory Between Fear and Flowers (2026), depicts a silent psychological confrontation between a contemporary woman and a man in primitive clothing, shaped by the past. He holds a rabbit, symbolizing unanalyzed fears and the masculine authority that society imposes, in which male vulnerability has no room to be expressed, while the woman clutches a miniature mirror image of herself. This reflection serves as an archive of maternal lineage, representing a future loved one, such as her daughter, and generations of inherited resilience. In addition to the main canvas, her exhibition includes six smaller dual-aspect portraits of faces. Together, these works examine how love, silence, and trauma are passed down through generations, creating a visual narrative that encourages women to liberate themselves from fears that weren’t theirs to begin with.
		
			
			
	Kimathi Mafafo at Kristin Hjellegjerde
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy the artist and Kristin Hjellegjerde				
					
				
	In a vibrant solo exhibition featuring seven intricate embroidered textile works, South African artist Kimathi Mafafo surveys nature as an embodied experience of female empowerment. Created with both hand and machine stitching, her works employ varied stitches that resemble rich brushstrokes, blending layers of pink, purple, and brown to achieve skin tones. Collaboration is central to Mafafo’s practice: She works closely with women she has trained in her studio, weaving elements of their lives into layered surfaces. This spirit of collective solidarity appears in Clearly, A Flamboyant Alliance: A Flamboyant Collaboration (2023), where overlapping limbs create a hybrid quality, as if the bodies are in motion. Drawing on childhood memories of visiting botanical gardens, Mafafo incorporates lush passion flowers into her tapestries. Her grandmother introduced her to this calming flower for its restorative properties, and it becomes a mystical transmitter of serenity. Mafafo’s sculptural fabrics offer a meditative quality, inviting introspection and nurturing energy that extends well beyond the canvas edges.

In art, as in life, the messy materiality of flesh fazes me not one whit.

	The climax of Lukas Moodysson’s A Hole in My Heart (2004), where Geko vomits into Tess’s open mouth? Wrote about it. Judy Chicago’s menstrual defiance, Ina Poppe’s mother’s milk cheese, Martin von Ostrowski’s spunk-strewn canvases, Marc Quinn’s sculpture cast with 10 pints of his own blood? Up my alley. Florentina Holzinger’s waste-processing, piss-wallowing Seaworld Venice at this year’s Austrian Pavilion? Love it.

	
		Related Articles
	


	Yet 20 minutes into a theatrical screening of Kristoffer Borgli’s The Drama (2026), I found myself in a posture of absolute misery: knees drawn to chest, shoulders hunched, the collar of my shirt pulled up under my eyes ready to cover them entirely, tension contorting my jaw. A body’s futile attempt to disappear into a single point. The proximate cause of all this anguish? A conversation among friends.
	

	The kids have a word for what happened here. So do the philosophers.

	Cringe. It’s a new term for an old thing.

	It bridges two affects: shame and sympathy. Shame is older—news to neither Eve nor Masaccio. From the root “to cover,” its mix of guilt, disgrace, and dishonor is bonded to castigation (think Andrea Büttner’s 2022–25 serigraphs of public humiliation), the vulnerability of nakedness (formalized in the extreme angle of Jenny Saville’s 1993 Plan), and the revelation of what ought to remain hidden (as in Tracey Emin’s 1995 Everyone I Have Ever Slept With 1963–1995 or Martine Syms’s diaristic 2020 photobook, Shame Space).


			
			
			
	
			
					Zendaya and Robert Pattinson in The Drama. 
									Courtesy A24
	



	In this painful experience, one is exposed (the betrayal that is blushing) and longs to hide oneself. Or obliterate the self—dying of shame is not always a metaphor.

	Sympathy comes later, unleashed in 18th-century thought through Adam Smith’s Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759). Secularizing and rationalizing the Christian law of Matthew 7:12 (“Do unto others” and all that), Smith insists that the imagination of an “impartial spectator” can form a conception of the emotional experience of another by representing how we would feel “if we were” in their situation: “We conceive ourselves enduring all the same torments, we enter, as it were, into his body, and become in some measure the same person with him.” And it is not merely that we can feel with others, but that we should: Smith is writing an ethics.
	

	Cringe is sympathetic shame. Vicarious embarrassment. Mortification by proxy.

	EVERY LANGUAGE HAS has a name for this unpleasant experience. In Dutch, plaatsvervangende schaamte is substitute shame. The French gêne par procuration delegates discomfort, while the German Fremdschämen means foreign shame.Swedish has the skämskudde, a “cringe cushion” in which to bury one’s face while watching, say, a globally televised breakdancing fail. In Japanese, mite irarenai means unable to look at something (distressing, awkward, disastrous), but it’s Chinese slang for the win with gāngà’ái: embarrassment cancer.

	These days, the interjection does a lot of work online as an all-purpose signifier of derogation. Policing cringe is the cruelest métier of the internet—the origin of harassment campaigns and platforming of contempt. The Four Horsemen of the digitally vulnerable—the queer, neurodivergent, economically precarious, and socially isolated—are far more likely to have their enthusiasms, efforts, and general being declared repellent or pathetic.

	Upon receiving an honorary degree in 2022, Taylor Swift urged graduates to “learn to live alongside cringe.” But we all know that while a pretty white girl’s earnestness may read as adorkable authenticity, that advice is tone-deaf at best, insensitive at worst to so many.
	

	Even in its less-noxious forms, to declare something “so cringe” is inherently censorious. “Hamilton is cringe!”flings Gen Alpha at their elders’ damp-eyed civic credulity; “Your nonsensical skibidi toilet rizz is cringe,” the millennials reply. Such generational accusations get tiresome quickly. Everyone thinks their kids’ slang is ridiculous and their parents’ politics naive.

	BUT BEHIND THE epithet’s online omnipresence is a serious aesthetic affect grouped among strong sensations that act on the body—terms like disgust (dis-taste: what one wants to spit out) or horror (from the Latin horrere: bristling hair). Its flinching recoil derives from the Old English cringan: to yield or fall (as in battle), eventually suggesting crouching in fear.

	While disgust claims the stomach and horror the nape, cringe assails the muscles of the face: a spectacle half-watched through half-narrowed eyes above a half-opened rictus.

	Cringe’s temporality is complex. Wincing—its signature gesture—is sharp, sudden, violent. But duration turns the screw—prolonged humiliation or a slow unfolding toward future self-recrimination.

	Is the cringeworthy utterly individual? Yes and no.

	It is like obscenity, in that you know it when you see it—except when you don’t and find yourself repelled or turned on by something self-evidently arousing or repulsive to someone else, and feel yourself exposed in having failed to have known it when you saw it.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Torbjørn Rødland: This Is My Body, 2013–15.
									©Torbjørn Rødland/Courtesy David Kordansky Gallery
	



	Cringing can therefore manifest as the abashment of not knowing (yet; possibly ever) how to read something. Most harrowing in Torbjørn Rødland’s This Is My Body (2013–15)—a luminous photograph of a girl’s head tilted upward by adult male hands whose fingers caress the edge of her mouth—is the realization that we cannot know whether we are witnessing bliss or brutality.

	In Diego Marcon’s video The Parents’ Room (2021), a prosthetically masked man sings of the murders of his wife and children, then of his suicide. The video plays hopscotch with tone—at once horrific, ridiculous, and bathetically earnest. To mock or to mourn? That is the (distressing) question.

	Or consider Jordan Strafer’s trilogy—Loophole (2023), Decadence (2024), and Talk Show (2026)—the last of which was shown in this year’s Whitney Biennial. It traffics in the somber content of trauma and sexual assault, yet performances are stylized beyond even the clichés of melodrama. Guiltily, we wonder: Are these testimonial figures worthy of compassion or not?


			
			
			
	
			
					Still from Diego Marcon’s film The Parents’ Room, 2021.
									Courtesy A24
	



	Complicating matters, one person’s cringe is another’s enjoyment. If X thinks some event will never befall them, or if they disallow any similarity to Y, then X might relish the spectacle of Y’s mortification—this is schadenfreude. If, however, I feel sympathy with Y on any grounds, then their humiliation is mine as well.
	

	The playwright Aristophanes’ account of love was the soul’s clocking of its like in another. As goes eros, so goes shame. To cringe is to recognize.

	Cringe thereby exposes a political truth: With whom do we feel we share something in common? It is an aesthetic reaction that strips bare one’s ethics of identification.

	NOT ALL ART THAT discomfits is cringe. Damien Hirst’s A Thousand Years (1990) confronts viewers with its vitrine containing a severed cow’s head and maggots-cum-flies. It may turn stomachs, but it lacks the minefield of social relationality.

	Although one can be ashamed of one’s former self (give the teenage poet a decade), cringe is inherently interpersonal, bound up with anxieties around social rejection. It scripts the interrogatory diagram where the collective meets the psychic: How do others regard me? As a joke? As talented? As a freak, a threat, an object of desire? A “chilled-out entertainer” of a boss? Da Ya Think I’m Sexy? Do you think I’m cool?

	The Drama staged this structure in the process of fracturing. Dining with her fiancé and close friends, a woman imagines she is speaking within a shared set of social norms as they each playfully admit the “worst thing” they’ve ever done. But at her turn, it becomes clear that she has revealed the wrong sort of vulnerability. In place of the intimacy that the other revelations engender, hers marks her as different. What ensues is the complete batshit breakdown of every form of relationality in the film.
	

	Nor is that all. The pain of cringe compounds. In my disturbance—whether witnessed by a fellow cinema patron or a reader of this essay—I am exposed a second time. In unconcealing what you find cringeworthy, cringe is secondhand shame that yields a firsthand confession.

	For my body has betrayed that my personal Room 101 must be the mid-exposure realization of having miscalculated a mutual understanding.


			
			
			
	
			
					Jordan Strafer’s installation Talk Show, 2026, in the Whitney Biennial.
									Photo Ron Amstutz/Courtesy Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
	



	LODGED IN THIS GAP between one’s self–image and someone else’s perception, all cringe art is, on some level, performance art.

	The School of Athens for first-generation cringe therefore includes 1970s body art (Abramović and Acconci, our deputized Plato and Aristotle), the anti-comedy of Andy Kaufman, and Viennese Actionism. Its iteration in the 1980s and 1990s includes some YBAs (Sarah Lucas) and the sick aesthetics of Paul McCarthy and Mike Kelley—witness the glorious banner reading pants shitter & proud p.s. jerk-off too (and i wear glasses) of Kelley’s 1987 Three Point Program/Four Eyes. Ryan Trecartin is the manic heir apparent to this trash-culture bloodline, updating it for a hyperperformative age.

	In the term’s modern era, media scholars point to an influential run of “cringe comedy” in quality television in the 2000s. The aughts had the fraternity of Curb Your Enthusiasm, Da Ali G Show, The Office (UK), and Peep Show. A decade later saw the feminist rejoinder: The Comeback, Girls, Veep, Crazy Ex-Girlfriend, Insecure, and Fleabag.
	

	In this golden age of cringe, that earlier art of transgression—with its tense silences, humiliations, and hostile disturbance of the performer-audience relationship—was channeled downstream. One could program the Girls Q-tip scene alongside Abramović’s Rhythm 0. And although they might not have the cultural capital of Acconci’s now-canonical Seedbed—in which he masturbated under a ramp while detailing his fantasies of the visitors walking above him—shows like Nathan for You and The Rehearsal have allowed Nathan Fielder to make a career off the same unwilled voyeurism experienced by those gallery visitors of 1972.

	THE EXPRESSIVE POSSIBILITIES of cringe have been subsequently taken up by a range of artists working today. But first, an important distinction.

	There is what I’ll call minor cringe—art that is about cringe but consumable with nary a wince. Minor cringe is meta-cringe, standing apart from the affect while coolly investigating it.

	Major cringe, on the other hand, navigates the aesthetic affect critically and formally to induce it—viscerally exploiting its possibilities. Major cringe is endo-cringe. It is within it; totally saturated by it.

	A Geschämtkunstwerk, if you will.

	The distinction is piece by piece; the same artist can produce both. Christine Tien Wang’s photorealistic meme paintings in her 2022 exhibition “Fake Stupid, queen of cringe” at Galerie Nagel Draxler in Berlin were minor cringe. Taking a bird’s-eye view of the affects of network culture—shame, snark, anxiety—they were, nevertheless, affectively innocuous.
	

	Not so with Starving Artist (2025), a canvas depicting a computer screen with multiple windows: a spreadsheet of bitcoin investments; the spine of a James Joyce novel; a meme based on the film Challengers; and an archival photograph of a victim of famine. Wang’s acrylic (re)rendering forces a reckoning with the moral stakes of algorithmic flattening. Shame is platformed. A portrait of collective responsibility for elisions between historical trauma and its ironized circulation? Major cringe.

	Nor does an artist progress from one to the other; they are merely different modes. Amalia Ulman’s 2025 film Magic Farm, about an American team’s desperation to manufacture a viral trend in rural Argentina, is minor cringe for its pleasurable skewering of the attention economy. Her Instagram long-form project Excellences & Perfections, from 2014, however, was major cringe. Why? Because its documentation of an extreme makeover in the vernacular of online self-modification involved aspects that were fabricated (her staged breast augmentation) and nonfabricated (her actual extreme food restriction). Vicarious disturbance bleeds into complicity in an era when self-representation is conflated with self-branding. There is no position outside of cringe here.

	ANY HUMILIATION IS a fall—the term descends from humilis, “on the ground.” Accordingly, many modern-day interlocutors of cringe are infatuated with the grotesque performative contortions required by life as a woman. Elevated ideals can only crumble.
	

	Several of those dragomans were included in the recent exhibition “Picture Perfect” at Bozar in Brussels, which ran from March to August of this year. The show sought to expand norms of representation—a project whose sincerity all but courts the cringeworthy—with artists hell-bent on deconstructing the drive for beauty, including Orlan, Sara Cwynar, Juno Calypso, and Haley Morris-Cafiero. Their works render femininity disgustingly cute, violently expressed, and contemptuously received by others—both when it fails and when it succeeds. Ideals are nightmares that way.

	Marianna Simnett’s video Blue Moon (2022) was on display: a glitching, flute-playing, Athena-like figure continuously morphing into a teal-and-tawny palette. Athena is herself an allegory about cringe—as the story goes, she abandoned and cursed her beloved flute after seeing how her cheeks puffed out while playing. That a self-image forged in the crucible of the fear of being ugly makes women amputate their talents? Sixteenth century BCE, meet 2026.


			
			
			
	
			
					Marianna Simnett: Blue Moon, 2022.
									Courtesy Société, Berlin
	



	Or regard Anna Uddenberg’s sculpture Focus #2 (Pussy Padding), 2018, on display at the Boros Collection in Berlin from 2022 to 2026. It assembles acrylic nails, resin and fiberglass, vinyl film, and a barstool to construct a female body bent in half as she extends a fake-fur–covered selfie stick over plastic-vented genitalia. The work is tacky in signifiers, excruciating in implication. The materials are the point: The more strictly synthetics are enlisted to illustrate a ludicrous eroticism, the more embarrassed we are to recognize the deforming desire to be desired.
	

	The apotheosis of this aesthetic of thirstiness is found in the paintings of Catherine Mulligan. Her solo show “Bad Girls Club” at Tara Downs in 2023 featured grotesque women seductively posed, decked out in the mien of late-millennial glam-trash McBling. The hands are a masterclass in contrast: Elongated nails resemble girlie self-care and melting flesh. Pouting lips are blow-job ready and corpse-bloated, flesh so bronzed it’s purple-gray. These half-dead bodies are so desperate for the world’s approval that their forms distort the pictorial, skewing perspective and leaching collaged text onto the sides of the frames.


			
			
			
	
			
					Catherine Mulligan: Bridge and Tunnel, 2023.
									Courtesy Tara Downs, New York
	



	Despite its bond with performance, cringe finds its medial match in such figurative painting. No accident that the likes of Lisa Yuskavage, Sasha Gordon, and Mulligan are regularly invoked in accounts of cringe-adjacent concepts like abjection, disturbance, disquiet. These painter’s painters retain a bond to recognizable forms of the real. To the extent that cringe feeds off sympathy and recognition, it blossoms where tropes, figures, and types play.

	One can thus imagine a shocking or rage-inducing abstract painting—the history of iconoclasm attests to this. But it is impossible to imagine a purely abstract painting in relation to cringe except as a bland metaphor for dislike. Cringe qua cringe is tethered to the social. It is most acute where it is most iconic.
	

	BEING THAT NETWORK culture is a constant inducement to exhibitionism, the internet is an incubator for public humiliation suo nomine. Accordingly, it has exponentially expanded the possibilities for humiliation by proxy.

	Made early in this era, Elisa Giardina Papa’s need ideas!?! PLZ!! (2011) is a compilation of YouTube clips of young teenagers attempting to generate viewership for their vlogs. Addressing the camera, guileless eyes above baby-fat cheeks entreat: “Hey uhm YouTube, it’s PinkSummerCrush, uhm… I wanted to start a web show and I need ideas for it but I don’t know, like, any ideas.” Another whispers, “I don’t know what to do so give me ideas. I’m trying to get more stuff done. Please send me ideas… please.”


			
			
			
	
			
									Elisa Giardina Papa’s installation need ideas!?! PLZ!!, 2011, at Stadtgalerie, Bern.
	



	These implorations are issued from childish bedrooms with an innocence oblivious to innuendo: “I want to make you guys happy” pleads one; “I’ll do anything except for sticking something up my nose” says another. Some both beg for ideas and announce they have zero subscribers, importing the possibility that no one is watching at all.

	No flayed martyr has anything on a teenage girl. Her exposure is total—her vulnerability pleromatic.

	This is major cringe at its limit. Not merely due to sympathy for the tweens, nor from projecting some future time when the unerasable archive of this yearning might prove embarrassing.
	

	Rather, to live under platform capitalism is to recognize the disturbing manner in which human need has been redescribed as algorithmic entanglement. Pretend you haven’t heard these phrases before and bear their weight: Please like this. I’ll do anything. Follow me.

	Cringe names our ethical recognition of the stakes of emptying out these words.

	FINALLY, THE TOUCHIEST question—the one that touches on taste. What about art that makes one cringe with embarrassment at its existence? For some, it’s the intentional kitsch of Neo-Pop; for others, the whole Jay-Z/Marina Abramović thing. I’ll nominate luxury-brand collaborations—the artworld’s driest thirst trap.

	But can we learn something from art that makes us feel this way? Something, perhaps, about time? Historical time, that is.

	Recall Nikki S. Lee’s “Projects,” made between 1997 and 2001, in which she photographed herself passing among various social groups and subcultures. Perhaps you, like I, were around for its heyday.


			
			
			
	
			
					A photo from Nikki S. Lee’s series “The Hip Hop Project,” 2001. 
									©Nikki S. Lee/Courtesy Sikkema Malloy Jenkins, New York
	



	It is said that today’s poor taste is tomorrow’s high art. Cringe works in reverse: What was high art yesterday can seem like a lapse in taste today.

	For who can look now at the darkened face and box braids of the Korean American photographer in her “Hip Hop Project” without wincing? (Cue a second grimace for that title.) Conversations around racial caricature have evolved; what was edgy feels painfully passé.
	

	Yet we can learn from cringe, so long as we stay closer to Smith’s moral sentiments than online callout culture. For cringe instructs us in the humility of taste—of our aesthetic fashions, of how we ask aesthetics to do politics in certain moments. Cringing at a dated work of art is a reminder of the fragility of all of our judgments.

	It has become fashionable lately to condemn sympathy for appropriating the misery of others. I remain convinced, however, that there is no truly good alternative. The sympathetic shame of cringe is the price of sociality. We live among others and have the extraordinary capacity to sometimes suffer as they do.

	Who would want the callous world that successfully cloistered the feelings of others? Cringe may be excruciating, but post-cringe would be pure horror.

title: A Once-in-a-Lifetime Look Into America’s Most-Storied Art Couple
description: “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, is a once-in-a-lifetime gathering of more 120 works by America’s most sto
body:
“Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, is a once-in-a-lifetime gathering of more 120 works by America’s most storied art couple: Lee Krasner (1908–84) and Jackson Pollock (1912–56). Much has been said about them, with almost all the focus being on Pollock. A May auction made him the newest member of the $100 million club, and the 1991 Pulitzer Prize for Biography went to Jackson Pollock: An American Saga by Steven Naifeh and Gregory White. At 934 pages long, the book inspired the Hollywood film Pollock (2000), for which Marcia Gay Harden won Best Supporting Actress for her portrayal of Krasner.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Indeed, Krasner herself has been seen as a supporting character for too long. In 1981, Barbara Rose curated the exhibition “Krasner/Pollock: A Working Relationship” to undermine the dominant narrative that she was a second-tier artist and long-suffering helpmate to her legendary husband, proposing that their marriage was a complex, working partnership of artistic equals. But Rose never got Krasner out of Pollock’s shadow.

	A show that pays more attention to Krasner than Pollock (she outlived him by 28 years), “Past Continuous” is more daring, nuanced, and expansive than previous attempts because, finally, it treats them as equals. The exhibition starts with footage, a panoramic view of their unheated, two-story, shingled house and studio on Long Island, overlayed with historic stills of Pollock, Krasner, their dog Gyp, and their tamed crow, Caw Caw. This is where Krasner and Pollock lived for nearly 11 years, until Pollock killed himself and one of his passengers, Edith Metzger, while driving drunk, injuring his girlfriend, Ruth Kligman, too. At the time, Krasner was in Europe, distancing herself from her husband’s drinking and philandering.

	It was in this house, far from New York and his favorite watering hole, the Cedar Bar, that Pollock made his first storied drip paintings. He unrolled unprimed canvas onto the studio floor and worked horizontally, applying enamel and house paints with sticks and brushes but never touching the canvas. He was inspired to do this by the paintings of Janet Sobel (1893–1968), a self-taught Ukrainian-born artist. Her Milky Way (1945), which he saw at Peggy Guggenheim’s Art of This Century gallery in 1946, directly inspired his first drip painting, Galaxy, in 1947.
	

	Just two years later, a headline in the widely popular LIFE magazine asked “Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?” elevating him from little-known abstract painter to overnight celebrity. Its four photographs showed Pollock as a brooding, hyper-masculine figure smoking a cigarette and wearing paint-splattered jeans. Krasner is not mentioned; he is portrayed as a solitary male genius.


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. 
									Photo Anna-Marie Kellen; Courtesy The Met
	



	Subverting that myth, the Met show ambitiously resets the history of Abstract Expressionism, going a long way to reveal the complexity of their artistic relationship. The first gallery presents Krasner’s collage works from the mid 1950s, when Pollock was at an artistic impasse and spiraling out of control. Until now, we’ve only ever gotten the lamentable tragedy of Pollock’s decline sans the triumph of Krasner’s emergence from his shadow.

	This retelling proves that by the mid-’50s, Krasner is Pollock’s equal and deserved to be see on her own. In Bald Eagle (1955), Krasner collaged scraps of dark brown linen and unprimed canvas that she and Pollock discarded, including on the white shape in the middle of the painting that resembles a bird’s profile, where we see Pollock’s dripped black line. Incorporating work rejected by her and her husband, Krasner was reborn, like a phoenix, from the destruction.
	

	It’s an apt metaphor for Krasner’s entire life and career. Beset with doubts and periods of blockage, Krasner had to find constantly ways to move on and pursue a trajectory that was all her own, all while facing Pollock’s larger-than-life. Before she ever met Pollock, Krasner wrote these lines from Arthur Rimbaud’s poem A Season in Hell on her studio wall:

	To whom shall I hire myself out? What beast must I adore?What holy image is attacked? What hearts shall I break?What lie must I maintain? In what blood tread?

	Constantly restless and one tough cookie, Krasner understood how hard it was to maintain one’s integrity as an artist.

	After proposing that Krasner more than held her own, the curators take a more biographical approach, placing examples of their early work—from before they met—in the same gallery. It starts with his-and-hers self-portraits—Krasner’s, in graphite and crayon, (ca. 1929-30); Pollock’s, a muddy brown, moody impasto (ca. 1930–33)—and includes a selection of paintings from a group show they both exhibited in, “American and French Painting” (1942). Curated by the Russian émigré artist and theoretician John Graham, it saw Pollock and Krasner hung alongside Stuart Davis, Willem de Kooning, Picasso, and Henri Matisse. After seeing the show and not knowing who Pollock was, Krasner looked him up. The rest is history.
	

	The exhibition is filled with highpoints, from Pollock’s lyrically expansive masterpiece, Number 1, 1950 (Lavender Mist), to the recreation of Krasner’s groundbreaking exhibition at the Stable Gallery in 1955, which led the critic Clement Greenberg to proclaim her “a major addition to the American art scene of the era.” He later declared that with drip painting, Pollock had gotten past Cubism (meaning Picasso) and made the first great American paintings. Although Greenberg suggested that Krasner had taken collage (again Picasso) into a new American territory, he stopped short of being as laudatory as he was for her husband. It was this hierarchical thinking (or glass ceiling) that Krasner crashed against throughout her career.

	Using pieces she and Pollock destroyed, abandoned, or never finished, she created both a body of work all her own. In Blue Level and Desert Moon (both 1955), with their solid areas of blues and reds, respectively, Krasner constructed a vertical world that stood straight and sturdy, raw elements reaching beyond the painting’s top and bottom edges. The verticality of these works can be seen as an aspirational self-portrait in which destruction and rebirth are literally and metaphorically merged.


			
			
			
	
			
					Lee Krasner: The Seasons, 1957.
	



	The latter rooms of the exhibition are dominated by Krasner, who moves into new territory, while Pollock makes a handful of one-of-a-kind paintings, such as Portrait and a Dream and The Deep (both 1953). In her smartly vulgar The Seasons (1957), which extends nearly 17 feet, Krasner returns to the subject of rebirth one year after Pollock’s death, depicting abundant forms resembling genitalia. That boldness continued right up to Past Continuous (1976), her last monumental collage made of charcoal drawings she made while studying with Hans Hofmann.
	

	In the 20 years between, we see major works from every decade. Restless as ever, she kept doing something unexpected. Take Kufic (1965), a spare, contemplative painting whose title refers to the oldest style of Arabic calligraphy, underscoring Krasner’s long interest in writing and linear marks. Rising Green (1971) is another standout in her masterful career.

	The exhibition culminates with the Future Indicative (1977), collaging Krasner’s figure drawings. Krasner, self-critical and never fully satisfied with what she had done, made multiple masterpieces in paint and collage that stand on their own and resemble none of her contemporaries. Finally, Krasner is recognized for her powerful contribution to American art.

title: Ibrahim Mahama’s Most Ambitious Show Yet Is Headed to Paris—But Its Core Is in Ghana
description: Listen to Ibrahim Mahama speak, and he’s likely to credit his success to his community, which includes market women, weavers, craftsmen, studio assi
body:
Listen to Ibrahim Mahama speak, and he’s likely to credit his success to his community, which includes market women, weavers, craftsmen, studio assistants, railway workers, curators, professors, and fellow artists.

	The Ghanaian artist is quick to recognize their contributions when he receives one of the many awards he’s picked up recently. Ranked at the top of the influential ArtReview Power 100 list in 2025, he also won an Art Basel Gold Award that year and received the 2026 Arnold Bode prize. He was also recently named a chevalier of the French government’s Ordre des Arts et des Lettres; the honor was bestowed upon him in Ghana by Diarra Dime Labille, France’s Ambassador to the West African country.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	“We live and work in a community and nobody is an island by themselves. I built my practice based on the idea of collectivity and working with different collaborators,” Mahama explained in an interview with ARTnews. As an example, he cited the scornful and at times suspicious reactions of Mallam Atta market women in Accra when he started collecting worn-out jute sacks at the early stage of his career, especially because he was still in college when he began producing those works. (The works he produced using those sacks quickly gained him fame, with some memorably appearing in Okwui Enwezor’s Venice Biennale in 2015.) As he spent time with the market women, they came to understand what he was doing and continued supporting him, helping him collect the sacks that still recur in his art.

	“I think the artist is just a vessel, and I see myself as that vessel in order to put all these different things together to do the work that we do,” he added.

	Mahama has become one of the most internationally visible Ghanaian artists, showing his work at biennials and museums across the world, and directing his success back to Ghana: The money from the sales of Mahama’s work is directed toward building institutions that he founds, including the Tamale-based Red Clay Studio and the Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art. He’s also bought dilapidated or abandoned buildings, factories, and airplanes, and turned them into art and educational spaces, as he did with Nkrumah Voli-ni, also in Tamale.
	

	These projects, which Mahama called a “lifetime work,” breathe new life into collected materials, archives, industrial and national heritage. His work at times extends beyond Ghana to include international like with people like the Kenyan British artist Michael Armitage and his Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute. Learning from those conversations and becoming part of a large community expands the scope of what is possible is Mahama’s practice.

	On Thursday, Mahama will open yet another epic project: “The Harvest Season,” an exhibition at the Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain in Paris, whose entire building he will take over starting next week. The show is “the most ambitious exhibition I’ve done,” Mahama said.


			
			
			
	
			
					Ibrahim Mahama.
									Photo Christian Cassiel/Courtesy Barbican Centre
	



	Parliament of Ghosts, an ongoing installation made of discarded train seats, railway sleepers, school furniture, worn-out jute sacks, and government archives that premiered in 2019 will figure in the Fondation Cartier show in a new iteration that adds about 200 collected and restored royal stools from the Asante Empire.

	The idea, Mahama said, is to highlight a contradiction: These same stools, which are often looted before being exhibited in Western museums, are at times placed in glass cases. At the Fondation Cartier, people will have free access to them. He hopes this will invert questions around the return of African objects from Europe, asking: What happens when these stools are brought from Ghana to Europe as “living” objects and utilized for their original purpose, and not in museum cases or glasses? Doing so brings out the “the ghosts [and] histories” of these stools, creating an avenue for different conversations, he added.
	

	There’s also a new project created by Mahama for this exhibition centered on the Aboso Glass Factory, which was established in 1966 by Ghana’s first president, Kwame Nkrumah, as part of the country’s industrialization efforts, before he was overthrown in a coup in that same year. Titled Things Fall Apart, after the 1958 novel by Nigerian author Chinua Achebe, it is a reconstruction of the abandoned glass bottle manufacturing plant that Mahama purchased some two years ago with production funds from Fondation Cartier.

	The Paris installation is only a small part of the project, however, since the glass factory is being rebuilt in spaces including Red Clay Studio in Tamale and a British-era colonial building. When the Fondation Cartier exhibition ends, the factory will be returned to Ghana for permanent installation in Kumasi, where Mahama plans to build a new institution. He is also working with cinema owners and local craftsmen to explore the possibility of rebuilding some abandoned cinemas in the country.


			
			
			
	
			
					Nkrumah Volini, an art center that Mahama founded in Tamale, Ghana, in 2021.
									©Ernest Sackitey/Courtesy Red Clay
	



	In addition, a collection of works on the Ghanaian railway system will also be on display in the exhibition. A new textile installation using Ghanaian fabrics produced in northern Ghana, truck inner tubes, jute sacks, and found textiles will be hung across the arcades on the facades of the Fondation Cartier building.
	

	“There is a dialogue between this old building [constructed in the 1850s] and Ibrahim’s work, which addresses the history of the 19th century in Ghana, and the links between what was happening between Europe and West Africa at that time,” said Aby Gaye-Duparc, the curator of the exhibition.

	“What we really want to convey to the audience is that there are two sides of [Mahama]’s artistic practice,” said Gaye-Duparc. “There’s work that we see: installations, videos, work on paper. Everything comes from this community in Tamale that he has built because a lot of the installations were made first in Tamale and then travel to Paris or other venues.”

	The other part, Gaye-Duparc continued, “is the work behind it that is being built in Tamale,” referring to the artist’s building of artistic infrastructure and institutions in the Northern Ghana city. These structures, she added, have expanded access to the arts for people who were left out for various reasons.

	In line with Mahama’s collaborative approach, the Paris exhibition will also feature work by artists and collectives including James Barnor, Gideon Appah, CATPC (Cercle d’Art des Travailleurs de Plantation Congolaise), Tjaša Rener, Postbox Ghana, Courage Dzidula Kpodo, and Dorothy Akpene Amenuke, Mahama’s mentor.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					A 1970s postcard showing Queen Elizabeth II Hall in Kumasi. The postcard is included in an archive maintained by Postbox Ghana, a participant in Mahama’s Fondation Cartier show.
									©Frederick Printing
	



	Kpodo, an architect, will exhibit work that addresses modernism, turning the focus away from tropical modernism centered on concrete buildings, which were often built by foreigners in Ghanaian cities. The central piece will be a wall reconstruction made out of laterite from a building he owns in Gyampo, in the Eastern Region, used in so-called vernacular or traditional buildings. The installation will include about 100 postcards by the Postbox Ghana collective depicting tropical modernist architectural buildings in cities such as Accra, Kumasi and Takoradi.

	“I would describe Ibrahim as someone who makes space within his own abilities and means for people that he thinks are doing interesting, important work,” said Kpodo.

	The Fondation Cartier exhibition is one of the first major ones by Mahama staged since he was viciously attacked earlier this year by a special operations unit of the Ghana Police Service in Tamale, where he lives and works. Mahama noted the community support that he received during the fallout, saying, “It was fantastic, I must say. I was really overwhelmed, because sometimes you don’t realize how much your work means to people.” He added that people traveled from within Tamale and from other cities like Accra and Kumasi came to visit him, express regret, and bemoan the treatment meted out to him by the police, especially because of his considerable contributions to the city.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Ibrahim Mahama, Season of Migration to the North, 2025–26.
									©Ibrahim Mahama/Photo ©Ernest Sackitey/Courtesy Red Clay
	



	He said he was unaware of the current state of the investigations into the matter by the Criminal Investigation Department as directed by Ghana’s Inspector General of Police because he hadn’t received updates in months. But he also seemed more interested in concentrating on his art. “I want to channel my energy into this positive part of my practice of what I do and what it means to the community,” he explained. “But certainly, I am also quite disappointed in the way that it was handled by the police. And I hope that at some point, we will be able to at least know more [about the investigations], so that we see what direction to take it in.” He plans to follow up again when he settles back in Ghana by the end of the year from his travels.

	For now, he is more focused on supporting the community he has helped create. “I’m happy that the work I do has a very profound meaning and effect on people who live on our continent, in particular Ghana. I am also interested in how this work is traveling around the world, stretching the African sensibilities, and what we are bringing to art in the 21st century.”

schema.headline: Ibrahim Mahama’s Most Ambitious Show Yet Is Headed to Paris—But Its Core Is in Ghana
